config.title: Implement Queue using Stacks

intro.title: Implement Queue using Stacks
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a queue data structure using two stacks. You will learn how to simulate the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) behavior of a queue by manipulating stacks, which follow a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) order. The main technologies involved are JavaScript arrays to represent stacks and functions to implement queue operations like enqueue and dequeue. This exercise will help you understand how data structures can be composed and the importance of algorithmic thinking in lesson-solving.
intro.usecase: The 'queue using stacks' pattern is essential in software where operations must be processed in a strict first-in, first-out (FIFO) order, but the underlying system or library only provides stack-like (LIFO) data structures. A concrete example is in web browser history management: when you navigate back and forward, the browser maintains a history stack, but simulating a linear back/forward queue (like a session history list) can require this dual-stack approach. Similarly, in UI frameworks, undo/redo functionality often uses two stacks to manage command history, effectively creating a queue of reversible actions. This pattern also appears in job schedulers or print spoolers where tasks are enqueued but might need reversal or reordering, requiring efficient FIFO simulation with stack primitives.

objectives: Construct a queue class using two stack data structures
Implement the enqueue operation by manipulating stack elements
Configure the dequeue operation to maintain FIFO order using stacks
Initialize stack instances within the queue class constructor
Apply stack methods to simulate queue behavior
Manipulate element transfer between stacks during operations
Control the state of both stacks to ensure correct queue functionality

content.body: We're going to build a queue using only stacks! This is a classic puzzle that helps you understand how data structures work under the hood. By the end, you'll implement a queue with stack operations only.
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
• Explain the difference between stack (LIFO) and queue (FIFO) behavior
• Implement a queue using two stacks
• Understand when to use push vs pop operations
• Analyze the cost of enqueue and dequeue operations
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Imagine you're at a cafeteria. People line up to get food - the first person in line gets served first (queue behavior). Now imagine stacking plates - you take from the top of the stack, which was the last plate added (stack behavior). How could you serve people first-in-first-out using only plates that follow last-in-first-out?
content.title: Think about it

content.body: Let's say we have two stacks of plates (Stack A and Stack B). People arrive in this order: Alice, Bob, Charlie. If we put them all on Stack A (push Alice, push Bob, push Charlie), we get Charlie on top. How could we serve Alice first using only stack operations (push/pop)?
content.title: Try it out

content.body: You probably realized that if we pop everything from Stack A and push to Stack B, the order reverses! Charlie (last in) goes to the bottom of Stack B, and Alice (first in) ends up on top of Stack B. Now we can pop from Stack B to serve Alice first.
content.title: What you discovered

content.body: But what if new people arrive while we're serving? We can't keep reversing stacks back and forth - that would be inefficient. We need a smarter way to handle both enqueue (adding) and dequeue (removing) operations efficiently.
content.title: The challenge

content.body: The mental model: Stack = last in, first out (like plates). Queue = first in, first out (like a line). To build a queue with stacks, we'll use two stacks: one for incoming items (enqueue stack) and one for outgoing items (dequeue stack). When the dequeue stack is empty, we'll transfer all items from enqueue stack to dequeue stack (reversing the order).
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like a restaurant with two counters: one where orders come in (enqueue stack), and one where orders go out for serving (dequeue stack). When the serving counter is empty, you bring all waiting orders over in reverse order.

content.body: We'll create a Queue class with two arrays (acting as stacks). New items always go to the first stack (push). When we need to remove an item (pop), we check the second stack. If it's empty, we transfer all items from the first stack to the second (which reverses their order), then pop from the second stack. This gives us FIFO behavior using LIFO operations!
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Initialize two empty stacks (arrays)
2. Enqueue: push item to stack1
3. Dequeue: if stack2 is empty, pop all items from stack1 and push to stack2 (reversing order), then pop from stack2
4. Peek: similar to dequeue but without removing
5. Empty: check if both stacks are empty
content.title: How it works

steps.title: Create the Queue class
steps.instruction: Start by creating a class called MyQueue with a constructor that initializes two empty arrays. These will act as our stacks.
steps.hint: Use this.stack1 and this.stack2 in the constructor.
steps.expectedOutcome: A class definition with two stack properties
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the foundation for our two-stack queue.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure both stacks are initialized as empty arrays.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to create a class with two empty array properties.

steps.title: Implement push (enqueue)
steps.instruction: Add a push method that takes a value and adds it to the first stack (stack1). This represents adding an item to the queue.
steps.expectedOutcome: A push method that adds to stack1
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! New items now go to stack1, our enqueue stack.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. The method should take a value parameter and push it to stack1.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: push should add the value to this.stack1 using the array push method.

steps.title: Implement transfer between stacks
steps.instruction: Create a helper method called _transfer that moves all items from stack1 to stack2. This reverses their order, making the oldest item in stack1 become the newest (top) in stack2.
steps.hint: Use a while loop: while (this.stack1.length > 0) { this.stack2.push(this.stack1.pop()); }
steps.expectedOutcome: A method that transfers items from stack1 to stack2
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start. Make sure you're popping from stack1 and pushing to stack2 until stack1 is empty.
steps.feedbackWrong: The _transfer method should move all items from stack1 to stack2 using pop and push.

steps.title: Implement pop (dequeue)
steps.instruction: Add a pop method that removes and returns the front item. If stack2 is empty, call _transfer first,
steps.hint: Check if stack2 is empty, transfer if needed, then return stack2.pop()
steps.expectedOutcome: A pop method that returns the front item
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Remember to check if stack2 is empty and transfer from stack1 if needed.
steps.feedbackWrong: The pop method should: 1) check if stack2 is empty, 2) call _transfer if needed, 3) return stack2.pop().

steps.title: pop from stack2
steps.hint: Check if stack2 is empty, transfer if needed, then return stack2.pop()
steps.feedbackPartial: Review the instruction and try again.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the instruction and try again.

steps.title: Implement peek
steps.instruction: Add a peek method that returns the front item without removing it. The logic is similar to pop but without the final pop operation.
steps.hint: After transferring if needed, return the last element of stack2 without popping it.
steps.expectedOutcome: A peek method that returns the front item
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Peek should return stack2[stack2.length - 1] after ensuring stack2 has items.
steps.feedbackWrong: Peek should: 1) check if stack2 is empty and transfer if needed, 2) return the last element of stack2.

steps.title: Implement empty check
steps.instruction: Add an empty method that returns true if both stacks are empty, false otherwise.
steps.hint: Check if both stack1.length and stack2.length are 0.
steps.expectedOutcome: An empty method that checks both stacks
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good. The empty method should return true only when both stacks have no items.
steps.feedbackWrong: Empty should check if both stack1 and stack2 have length 0.

content.body: You've successfully implemented a queue using two stacks! Remember: stacks are LIFO (last in, first out) like plates, while queues are FIFO (first in, first out) like a line. The key insight is that transferring items between two stacks reverses their order, allowing us to simulate queue behavior. Use stacks when you need to track nested operations (like function calls or undo), and queues when you need to process items in arrival order (like tasks or requests).
content.title: Well done!
